---
title: Architecture
description: How the Quoin workspace is organized — the facade, the core traits, the adapter crates, and the shared machinery beneath them.
type: explanation
---

import { Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Quoin's architecture separates three concerns: a small trait contract, five adapters that implement it natively, and shared machinery that keeps the adapters consistent. Everything composes through the `quoin` facade crate.

## The layers

<Code lang="text" code={`        your app / your hook library
                    │
              quoin (facade)          ← feature flags pick one backend
        ┌─────────┼─────────┐
   quoin-macros  quoin-ui   quoin-core   ← contract + tooling
        │           │          │
   quoin-macros-core quoin-style      ← parsing & codegen
        │
   ┌────┴─────┬──────────┬───────────┬──────────┐
 quoin-gpui quoin-leptos quoin-dioxus quoin-xilem quoin-floem
        └──────────┴──────────┴─────┬─────┴──────────┘
                    shared machinery in quoin-core
              join · globals · NotifierSignal · batch · pool`} />

## The contract layer

`quoin-core` defines the traits every adapter implements: `Signal<T>`, `ReactiveContext`, `Executor`, plus the blanket extension traits (`SignalExt`, `ExecutorExt`, `ReactiveContextExt`) that are implemented once, generically, so every adapter gets them for free with zero per-adapter code. Portable conveniences also live here: derived/memo/zip, resources, batching, cancellation, `spawn_local`, timers, and pooling.

## The adapter layer

Each adapter crate (`quoin-gpui`, `quoin-leptos`, `quoin-dioxus`, `quoin-xilem`, `quoin-floem`) provides a concrete `ReactiveContext` for its framework. Adapters share machinery that used to be hand-copied five times:

- **join** — the `JoinHandle` lifecycle (await / abort / detach / abort-on-drop) is written once; only the "how do we cancel the underlying task" part differs per framework.
- **globals** — the thread-local, `TypeId`-keyed store behind `provide_global`/`use_global` on the pull-based adapters.
- **NotifierSignal** — the cell-plus-notifier signal implementation with batch awareness.

On `wasm32`, the Leptos and Dioxus executors run futures on the main thread via `wasm_bindgen_futures`; on native they use threads like the other adapters.

## The macro layer

`quoin-macros` is a thin `proc_macro` boundary over `quoin-macros-core`, which parses `component!`/`quoin_render!`/`effect!` once and emits per-backend code through `FrameworkEmitter` implementations. Class strings are parsed by `quoin-style` into a typed IR (`Decl` lists per state) — one parse, many lowerings, no runtime class parsing. Unrecognized classes become compile errors with did-you-mean suggestions.

## The protocol and tooling layer

- `quoin-ui` declares the Universal Component Protocol traits and node vocabulary; `quoin-ui-gpui` is the first full implementation.
- `quoin-testkit` supplies `TestContext` and deterministic executors for headless testing.
- `quoin-devtools` wraps any context with `Instrumented` and records events into a ring buffer.
- `quoin-conformance` holds the shared suite that every adapter must pass — the mechanism behind [backend parity](/explanation/backend-parity/).

## Facade composition

The `quoin` facade re-exports all of the above behind feature flags. Framework features are mutually exclusive (a `compile_error!` fires otherwise); `testkit` and `devtools` are additive. This keeps a typical application at one dependency line while letting framework-free libraries depend on `quoin-core` alone.

## Next steps

- <LinkCard title="The Reactivity Model" href="/explanation/reactivity-model/" description="How the contract maps onto pull-based and fine-grained frameworks." />
- <LinkCard title="Crates" href="/reference/crates/" description="The per-crate reference table." />


---

---
title: Backend Parity
description: How Quoin guarantees identical adapter behavior — the shared conformance suite, macro expansion tests, and the class-engine parity harness.
type: explanation
---

import { LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

"Works identically on every adapter" is a testable claim, and Quoin tests it from three directions: behavior, code generation, and styling.

## The conformance suite

`quoin-conformance` contains a shared suite of 30+ checks that every adapter must pass. The suite exercises the full shared contract: signals and `set_eq`, derived and memo behavior, batching, shared globals, the join-handle lifecycle (await / abort / detach / drop-cancels), `spawn_with_token`, cancellation cascades, and executor timers (`executor_sleep_resolves`, `executor_spawned_task_sleeps`). Adapter crates run the same suite in their own test targets — for example `just test-conformance-gpui` — and CI runs it for every adapter on every push.

Because the checks live in one suite rather than five hand-written test folders, a new behavior lands as one new check that immediately applies to all backends. The GPUI suite covers the full shared contract (31 checks, previously 19).

## Macro expansion testing

Three layers verify that one macro source produces correct code on each backend:

- `quoin-macros-tests` — trybuild UI tests that assert both successful expansions (GPUI, Leptos, Dioxus pass cases) and exact compiler diagnostics for invalid input (missing `render`, unknown elements, missing defaults, unexpected identifiers).
- `quoin-expand-test` — expansion snapshot testing via `just expand`.
- `quoin-grsx-compiletest` — compiles full engine expansions (new vocabulary, variants, dynamic classes, control flow, handlers) against the vendored GPUI stub so emitted builder chains type-check without building real GPUI.

## Class-engine parity

`interop-tests` is the parity harness for the GPUI class engine. It gates:

- **34/34 theme-token classes byte-identical** through gpui-rsx's `Theme`
- **The GPUI ⊇ web vocabulary-superset gate** — everything the shared parser accepts must lower on GPUI
- **The Tailwind-scale gate** — spacing utilities match the Tailwind 4 px scale
- The variant table, plus diagnostic probes

Under the `gpui-rsx-classes` flag, classes Quoin already knows keep their byte-identical lowering — the same parity tests verify it.

## What parity means for you

You can treat the adapter as an implementation detail. A hook that passes its conformance-backed contract — signals, effects, tasks, cancellation, globals — behaves the same whether the binary links GPUI or Leptos, which is what makes feature-flag re-targeting (the [tutorial's](/tutorials/build-a-counter/) final step) safe.

## Next steps

- <LinkCard title="The Reactivity Model" href="/explanation/reactivity-model/" description="What the conformance suite verifies about push vs pull adapters." />
- <LinkCard title="Testing with quoin-testkit" href="/guides/testing/" description="Apply the same rigor to your own hooks." />


---

---
title: The Reactivity Model
description: How Quoin's signal model works — tracking on fine-grained frameworks, notifications on pull-based ones, and what batching, memos, and resources do under the hood.
type: explanation
---

import { Aside, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Quoin's five adapters fall into two families, and the reactivity model is designed so one set of user code behaves correctly on both.

## Two families of frameworks

**Fine-grained (Leptos, Dioxus, Floem).** The framework tracks which signals a render scope reads and re-runs that scope when a tracked signal changes. Quoin's signal reads participate in the native tracking, so a `derived` signal's source read inside the derive closure is tracked by the reactive graph — any consumer reading the derived value in a reactive scope re-runs when the source changes.

**Pull-based (GPUI, Xilem).** The framework re-renders a component when it is notified. Quoin's signals call `request_update()` on mutation through the context notifier; the next render pulls fresh values, and derived signals recompute on their next read.

The same hook is correct on both because it never assumes push or pull: it writes through `Signal` methods and reads wherever it needs values.

## What each primitive does under the hood

**Signals.** The shared implementation is `NotifierSignal` in `quoin-core` — a cell plus a batch-aware notifier. Adapters may use it directly or wrap their native signal types; either way the trait surface (`get`/`set`/`update`/`with`/`set_if_eq`) is identical.

**Derived and memos.** `derived` recomputes the closure on every read; `Memo` remembers the last source value and caches its output until the source differs. On fine-grained frameworks tracking makes derived reads reactive; on pull-based ones the mutation-triggered re-render does the equivalent job.

**Batching.** A thread-local depth counter. Inside `batch::with`, pull-based signals consult `should_notify()` and skip their notifier calls; when the outermost batch ends, one `request_update()` fires. Fine-grained frameworks batch internally and ignore the mechanism, so calling `cx.batch` is always safe.

**Resources.** Built from a `Signal` holding `ResourceState` plus an `Executor` task. Each reload increments a generation counter; when a request completes it may only write its result if its generation is still current — that is what makes reloads race-free. The request also holds a `CancellationToken`, and the task is aborted through the executor's join handle, so a reload cancels the in-flight work both cooperatively (token) and structurally (abort).

**Globals.** A thread-local, `TypeId`-keyed map keyed by context type and value type. This matches the main-thread assumptions of GPUI, Xilem, and Floem; the fine-grained adapters map their own stores onto the same observable semantics — one shared cell per (context, type) pair.

**Local tasks.** On WASM, `spawn_local` delegates to `wasm_bindgen_futures::spawn_local` (browser main thread). On native, a `!Send` future cannot cross threads soundly, so tasks enter a thread-local FIFO queue and `run_local_tasks()` drives them one completion at a time — deterministic enough for tests.

<Aside type="note">
  The practical consequence: whether your app runs on a push-based renderer or a pull-based one, batching is an optimization (never a correctness fix), derived values are always consistent with their sources, and dropping a task handle always cancels the task.
</Aside>

## Next steps

- <LinkCard title="Backend Parity" href="/explanation/backend-parity/" description="How identical behavior is verified with a shared conformance suite." />
- <LinkCard title="Batched Updates" href="/reference/batching/" description="The batching API reference." />


---

---
title: Why Quoin Exists
description: The problems Quoin solves — framework lock-in, untestable UI logic, and duplicated reactivity code across the Rust GUI ecosystem.
type: explanation
---

import { LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Building cross-platform Rust UI applications usually means choosing a framework and being locked into its reactivity model. GPUI, Leptos, Dioxus, Xilem, and Floem each define their own signal systems, task spawners, and state idioms. A search box, a todo store, or a data-fetching pipeline written for one of them cannot run on another.

## The four problems

**Write once, run anywhere.** The same reactive hooks — signals, derived values, async tasks — should work in GPUI, Leptos, Dioxus, Xilem, and Floem. Quoin defines those primitives once, as traits, and each framework adapter implements them.

**Test in isolation.** UI logic that is welded to a framework is hard to test: you spin up windows or browsers to exercise a counter. Quoin decouples business logic from the view layer, so you mock a `ReactiveContext` — or use the headless `quoin-testkit` — and test with plain `cargo test`.

**Switch frameworks without rewriting logic.** Change a feature flag and recompile; your hooks stay unchanged. The view layer is the only thing you rewrite, and the declarative macros shrink that too.

**Share libraries.** Framework-agnostic crates that work with any Quoin-supported UI can be published and reused — the counter hook in the [tutorial](/tutorials/build-a-counter/) is one example, and `todo-core` and `fetch-core` in the repository are tested, end-to-end examples of the pattern.

## The design stance

- **Traits over wrappers.** Quoin does not hide the frameworks; it defines the smallest common contract (`Signal`, `ReactiveContext`, `Executor`) and lets adapters optimize natively.
- **Compile-time selection.** Exactly one framework feature is enabled per crate, enforced with `compile_error!`. There is no runtime dispatch and no hidden priority between backends.
- **Parity is tested, not assumed.** A shared conformance suite runs 30+ checks per adapter, so "works identically everywhere" is a CI gate rather than an aspiration.
- **No unsafe code.** The workspace forbids `unsafe` outright and runs pedantic Clippy with warnings as errors.

## What Quoin is not

It is not a rendering framework, a widget toolkit replacement, or a virtual DOM. Rendering stays native to each framework; Quoin owns the reactive layer beneath it, plus optional declarative macros that emit native view code per framework.

## Next steps

- <LinkCard title="Build a Cross-Framework Counter" href="/tutorials/build-a-counter/" description="See the decoupling in action end to end." />
- <LinkCard title="Architecture" href="/explanation/architecture/" description="How the crates and adapters are organized." />

---
title: Loading Async Data
description: Fetch remote data with race-free resources, spawn async tasks on the framework runtime, and use portable timers.
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

You will load remote data into the UI without races between stale and fresh responses, and you will run background work on the framework's native async runtime.

**Prerequisites:** a working Quoin setup and a context that implements `ReactiveContext` (see [Writing Portable Hooks](/guides/portable-hooks/)).

## Load data with a resource

`cx.create_resource` gives every adapter the async-data lifecycle familiar from Leptos and Dioxus: `Idle → Loading → Ready(T) | Failed(E)`. Pass a closure that receives a [`CancellationToken`](/reference/cancellation/) and returns a future:

<Code lang="rust" code={`let user = cx.create_resource(|token| async move {
    // Check the token between awaits so reloads stop stale work:
    Ok::<User, FetchError>(fetch_user(&token).await?)
});

// Anywhere in the UI:
match user.state().get() {
    ResourceState::Ready(user) => render_user(&user),
    ResourceState::Loading => render_spinner(),
    ResourceState::Failed(err) => render_error(&err),
    ResourceState::Idle => render_placeholder(),
}`} />

The resource handles the two problems that plague hand-rolled fetch loops:

- **Race-free reloads** — every reload bumps a generation counter, so a stale request can never overwrite a newer result.
- **Cooperative cancellation** — reloading cancels the in-flight request through its token and aborts the task through the executor's join handle.

Call `user.reload_with(&cx, fetch)` to re-run the fetch closure; the state returns to `Loading` until the new request settles.

## Spawn one-off tasks

For work that is not tied to a resource, spawn onto the framework runtime with the executor:

<Code lang="rust" code={`let handle = cx.executor().spawn(async {
    let data = fetch_from_api().await;
    signal.set(data);
});

// Later: await the result (Err(Canceled) if aborted), abort(), or detach().`} />

Every adapter implements the same join-handle lifecycle:

| Operation | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `handle.await` | Waits for the result; the task runs to completion. |
| `handle.abort()` | Cancels at the next suspension point; later awaits resolve with `Err(Canceled)`. |
| `handle.detach()` | Fire-and-forget; the task runs to completion, its result is discarded. |
| `drop(handle)` | Cancels the task — structured concurrency, no orphaned tasks mutating UI state. |

Cancellation is cooperative on the thread-based adapters (Leptos, Dioxus, Floem): the future stops at its next `.await` point. GPUI and Xilem cancel natively.

## Fetch-and-cancel in one call

`spawn_with_token` (from `ExecutorExt`, in the prelude) creates a cancellation token and hands it to your future:

<Code lang="rust" code={`let (handle, token) = cx.executor().spawn_with_token(|t| async move {
    while !t.is_cancelled() {
        do_work().await;
    }
});
// User navigated away:
token.cancel();`} />

## Run !Send futures with spawn_local

Browsers run WASM on a single thread and most DOM-touching futures are `!Send`. The `LocalExecutor` machinery covers both worlds:

<Code lang="rust" code={`use quoin_core::LocalExecutor;

cx.executor().spawn_local(async { update_dom().await });`} />

- **On `wasm32`** tasks run on the browser main thread via `wasm_bindgen_futures`.
- **On native** tasks enter a deterministic thread-local FIFO queue driven by `quoin_core::local::run_local_tasks()` — useful in tests.

<Aside type="caution">
  GPUI does not implement `LocalExecutor` — its executor is `!Send` by design. Use `Executor::spawn` there.
</Aside>

## Sleep without an async runtime

Timers are part of the executor contract. `executor.sleep(duration)` returns a future on every adapter (futures-timer on native, browser timers on WASM), and the free function `quoin_core::sleep` gives you a standalone `SyncSleepFuture`:

<Code lang="rust" code={`cx.executor().sleep(Duration::from_millis(250)).await;`} />

## Next steps

- <LinkCard title="Cancelling Work" href="/guides/cancelling-work/" description="Child tokens, RAII guards, and racing work against cancellation." />
- <LinkCard title="Resources Reference" href="/reference/resources/" description="The full Resource and ResourceState API." />
- <LinkCard title="Executors & Tasks Reference" href="/reference/executors/" description="Spawn, join handles, local tasks, and timers." />

---
title: Cancelling Work
description: Cancel long-running async work cooperatively with child tokens, RAII guards, and run-until-cancelled races.
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

You will stop work that is no longer wanted — abandoned searches, closed panels, superseded polls — using Quoin's cancellation toolkit, which behaves identically on all five adapters.

**Prerequisites:** familiarity with spawning tasks ([Loading Async Data](/guides/async-data/)).

## Poll the token

`CancellationToken` is cloneable and cheap. The most direct pattern checks it inside a loop:

<Code lang="rust" code={`let token = CancellationToken::new();
executor.spawn({
    let token = token.clone();
    async move {
        while !token.is_cancelled() {
            do_work().await;
        }
        cleanup().await;
    }
});

// Later, from another task or UI event:
token.cancel();`} />

Cancellation is **cooperative**: nothing preempts your future. It stops at its next suspension point, so long computations between `.await`s delay it.

## Await cancellation itself

`token.cancelled()` returns a future that resolves when the token fires; `into_cancelled()` gives an owned variant. Use them to select between completion and shutdown:

<Code lang="rust" code={`tokio::select! {
    result = work() => handle(result),
    _ = token.cancelled() => shutdown().await,
}`} />

## Race work against cancellation

`run_until_cancelled` resolves with `Some(output)` when the wrapped future finishes first, or `None` when the token wins:

<Code lang="rust" code={`let value = token.run_until_cancelled(work()).await;
match value {
    Some(result) => apply(result),
    None => /* cancelled */,
}`} />

## Build token trees

Long-lived screens create child tokens that cancel together with their parent but also cancel independently:

<Code lang="rust" code={`let parent = CancellationToken::new();
let per_request = parent.child_token();  // cancels with the parent
// Cancelling per_request leaves parent untouched.
// Cancelling parent also cancels per_request.`} />

This models UI lifetimes: one parent token per view, one child per in-flight request.

## Cancel on drop with guards

`guard()` returns an RAII guard that cancels the token when dropped — the "cancel when this scope exits" pattern:

<Code lang="rust" code={`let token = CancellationToken::new();
let _guard = token.guard();  // token.cancel() runs when _guard drops`} />

## Detach or drop — know the difference

Dropping a join handle cancels the task; that is structured concurrency by default. When you genuinely want fire-and-forget, call `detach()` explicitly so the task runs to completion:

<Code lang="rust" code={`let handle = executor.spawn(log_flusher());
handle.detach();  // survives; drop(handle) would have cancelled it`} />

<Aside type="tip">
  Prefer drop-cancellation. A task that mutates UI state after its view is gone is a bug class Quoin's defaults eliminate.
</Aside>

## Next steps

- <LinkCard title="Cancellation Tokens Reference" href="/reference/cancellation/" description="Every method and future type on CancellationToken." />
- <LinkCard title="Loading Async Data" href="/guides/async-data/" description="Resources with built-in race-free reloads and cancellation." />

---
title: Tracing with quoin-devtools
description: Record every signal mutation, task spawn, and update request with quoin-devtools, then inspect the log at runtime or on exit.
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

You will instrument a running application to see what its reactive core is doing: signal creations, read-triggering mutations, update requests, and task spawns, completions, and aborts. `quoin-devtools` wraps **any** adapter's context — GPUI, Leptos, Dioxus, Xilem, Floem, or the testkit context.

**Prerequisites:** the `devtools` feature (or a direct dependency on `quoin-devtools`).

## Wrap the context

`Instrumented::wrap` is a drop-in wrapper: keep using the wrapped context everywhere you used the raw one.

<Code lang="rust" code={`use quoin_devtools::Instrumented;

let raw_ctx = /* any adapter context */;
let ctx = Instrumented::wrap(raw_ctx, "app");`} />

## Enable recording

Recording is gated so that shipping the wiring costs nothing when disabled — with tracing off, each call is one relaxed atomic load and nothing is allocated.

<Code lang="sh" code={`QUOIN_TRACE=1 ./myapp    # or QUOIN_TRACE=on`} />

Alternatively enable it programmatically: `quoin_devtools::enable()` (and `disable()` / `enabled()` to inspect the state).

## Read the log

The global `EventLog` is a ring buffer (default capacity 4096 events) with three aggregate views:

<Code lang="rust" code={`quoin_devtools::global_log().dump();          // stderr table
quoin_devtools::global_log().hot_signals();   // ranked mutation counts
quoin_devtools::global_log().events();        // raw snapshot of Event values`} />

Call them from a debug hotkey, a drop-down panel, or on exit. Each event carries an `EventKind` (updates, spawns, mutations, …) and the label you passed to `Instrumented::wrap`.

## See it live in a real window

The `counter-xilem` example renders trace counts next to the counter and dumps the session when the window closes:

<Code lang="sh" code={`cargo run --manifest-path examples/counter-xilem/Cargo.toml`} />

For a headless tour of the tracing session itself, run `just trace-demo` (it drives `devtools-demo` with `QUOIN_TRACE=1`).

## Forward to the tracing ecosystem

The optional `tracing` feature forwards events into the [`tracing`](https://crates.io/crates/tracing) ecosystem instead of (or in addition to) the built-in log.

<Aside type="tip">
  Pair devtools with the testkit in CI: an `EventLog` snapshot makes a useful assertion surface — for example, that a feature flag flip caused exactly one update request.
</Aside>

## Next steps

- <LinkCard title="quoin-devtools Reference" href="/reference/devtools/" description="Every public item: Instrumented, EventLog, EventKind, and the record helpers." />
- <LinkCard title="Testing with quoin-testkit" href="/guides/testing/" description="Deterministic headless testing of the same reactive code." />

---
title: Sharing Global State
description: Store app-wide state with provide_global and use_global, update it safely, and understand the shared-cell semantics.
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

You will store application-wide values — theme, settings, a router state — outside any single component and access them from any hook or view.

**Prerequisites:** a context implementing `ReactiveContext` (see [Writing Portable Hooks](/guides/portable-hooks/)).

## Provide and read a global

`provide_global` stores a value keyed by its type; `use_global` retrieves it as a reactive signal handle:

<Code lang="rust" code={`cx.provide_global(Theme::Dark);

if let Some(theme) = cx.use_global::<Theme>() {
    // theme is a signal handle — read or observe it.
    let current = theme.get();
}`} />

Store one value per type per context. Two adapters running on the same thread never collide: the underlying store keys entries by both the context type and the value type.

## Update a global in place

`update_global` (from `ReactiveContextExt`, in the prelude) mutates the stored value through a closure. The type parameter after the struct is your error type — return `Err` to reject the update:

<Code lang="rust" code={`cx.update_global::<Settings, ()>(|s| s.theme = Theme::Dark);`} />

## Initialize on first use

`use_global_or_init` inserts a default when no value exists yet and returns the handle either way:

<Code lang="rust" code={`let settings = cx.use_global_or_init(Settings::default);`} />

This replaces the provide-then-read dance for globals that always exist.

## Semantics on every adapter

All five adapters share one semantic: every `use_global` call returns a handle to the **same shared cell**, so a mutation performed through one handle is visible through every other handle. The pull-based adapters (GPUI, Xilem, Floem) back this with a thread-local, `TypeId`-keyed map matching each framework's main-thread assumptions:

- Globals are visible on the thread that registered them.
- GPUI, Xilem, and Floem share the same thread-local machinery from `quoin_core::globals`; the fine-grained adapters map onto their own stores with identical observable behavior.

<Aside type="caution">
  Globals live per thread on native targets. Register them on the main/UI thread and read them there; crossing threads is the job of signals passed through tasks, not of the global store.
</Aside>

## Next steps

- <LinkCard title="Reactive Context Reference" href="/reference/reactive-context/" description="The full ReactiveContext and ReactiveContextExt surface, including the global methods." />
- <LinkCard title="The Reactivity Model" href="/explanation/reactivity-model/" description="How signals, batching, and globals interact under the hood." />

---
title: Installation
description: Add Quoin to a Rust project, choose the right feature flags, and satisfy the system prerequisites for each framework adapter.
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard, TabItem, Tabs } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

This guide gets Quoin into an existing Cargo project and explains every feature flag you can enable. Quoin supports Rust 1.88 and newer (the workspace declares `rust-version = "1.88"`).

## Prerequisites

- Rust stable 1.88+ (`rustup update stable`).
- For the GPUI adapter on Linux: `libxkbcommon-dev`, `libx11-dev`, `libxcb1-dev`, `libwayland-dev`, and `libfontconfig1-dev`.
- The other adapters (Leptos, Dioxus, Xilem, Floem) have no system-library requirements beyond Rust itself.

## Add the dependency

Enable exactly **one** framework feature — this choice selects the adapter compiled into your binary:

<Tabs>
  <TabItem label="GPUI">
    <Code lang="sh" code={`cargo add quoin --features gpui`} />
  </TabItem>
  <TabItem label="Leptos">
    <Code lang="sh" code={`cargo add quoin --features leptos`} />
  </TabItem>
  <TabItem label="Dioxus">
    <Code lang="sh" code={`cargo add quoin --features dioxus`} />
  </TabItem>
  <TabItem label="Xilem">
    <Code lang="sh" code={`cargo add quoin --features xilem`} />
  </TabItem>
  <TabItem label="Floem">
    <Code lang="sh" code={`cargo add quoin --features floem`} />
  </TabItem>
</Tabs>

This is equivalent to editing `Cargo.toml`:

<Code lang="toml" code={`[dependencies]
quoin = { version = "0.1", features = ["gpui"] }`} />

<Aside type="caution">
  Enabling two framework features on the same crate is a compile error. Quoin emits a `compile_error!` naming the mutually exclusive features rather than silently picking one.
</Aside>

## Library-only dependencies

If you are writing a shared hook or store crate that must stay framework-free, depend on `quoin-core` instead of `quoin`. It contains the traits and portable machinery with no adapter compiled in:

<Code lang="toml" code={`[dependencies]
quoin-core = "0.1"`} />

Consumers of your crate then pick the framework by enabling one feature on their `quoin` dependency and passing your hook any context that implements `ReactiveContext`.

## Feature flag matrix

| Feature | What it enables |
| --- | --- |
| `gpui` | GPUI adapter + UCP GPUI implementation + macros; implies `rsx` and `gpui-rsx-classes` |
| `leptos` | Leptos adapter + macros |
| `dioxus` | Dioxus adapter + macros |
| `xilem` | Xilem adapter + macros |
| `floem` | Floem adapter + macros |
| `macros` | `component!`, `quoin_render!`, `effect!`, `run_app!`, `quoin_element!` without a framework |
| `ui` | Universal Component Protocol traits from `quoin-ui` |
| `rsx` | gpui-rsx escape hatch (`rsx!`, `#[component]`, …) for GPUI-only subtrees |
| `gpui-rsx-classes` | Extended Tailwind engine for GPUI (full palette, more variants, dynamic `class:`) |
| `testkit` | Re-exports `quoin-testkit` for headless testing |
| `devtools` | Re-exports `quoin-devtools` for signal tracing |
| `leptos-shadcn` | shadcn component backing for the Leptos emitter (requires `leptos`) |
| `dioxus-shadcn` | shadcn component backing for the Dioxus emitter (requires `dioxus`) |
| `floem-shadcn` | shadcn component backing for the Floem emitter (requires `floem`) |

The full reference with dependencies between flags lives in [Feature Flags](/reference/feature-flags/).

## Verify the setup

Create a signal and read it back in a unit test using `quoin-testkit` — no window, no browser:

<Code lang="rust" code={`use quoin::prelude::*;
use quoin::testkit::{TestContext, ImmediateExecutor};

#[test]
fn signal_round_trip() {
    let cx = TestContext::with_executor(ImmediateExecutor);
    let count = cx.create_signal(0u32);
    count.set(42);
    assert_eq!(count.get(), 42);
}`} />

<Code lang="sh" code={`cargo test`} />

**Expected output:** the test passes, confirming the adapter compiled and the context works.

- <LinkCard title="Build a Cross-Framework Counter" href="/tutorials/build-a-counter/" description="The golden-path tutorial from zero to a running app." />
- <LinkCard title="Feature Flags Reference" href="/reference/feature-flags/" description="Every flag, its dependencies, and when to enable it." />

---
title: Writing Portable Hooks
description: Write reusable reactive hooks — signals, derived state, and effects — that compile unchanged on every Quoin adapter.
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

You will extract reactive business logic into hook functions that know nothing about the view framework. This is the core Quoin workflow: hooks depend only on the `ReactiveContext` and `Signal` traits, so the same function serves GPUI, Leptos, Dioxus, Xilem, and Floem.

**Prerequisites:** Quoin installed with one framework feature (see [Installation](/guides/installation/)).

## Keep the hook generic over the context

Write hooks as free functions generic over `C: ReactiveContext` and return your own struct so callers get a typed handle:

<Code lang="rust" code={`use quoin_core::prelude::*;
use std::rc::Rc;

pub struct SearchBox<S: Signal<String>> {
    pub query: S,
    pub clear: Rc<dyn Fn()>,
}

pub fn use_search<C: ReactiveContext>(cx: &C) -> SearchBox<C::Signal<String>> {
    let query = cx.create_signal(String::new());
    let clear = {
        let query = query.clone();
        Rc::new(move || query.set(String::new()))
    };
    SearchBox { query, clear }
}`} />

Import with `use quoin_core::prelude::*;` (framework-free crates) or `use quoin::prelude::*;` (application crates). The prelude includes the extension traits, so `.map()`, `set_eq()`, and `create_resource()` are available without extra imports.

## Compute values with derived signals

Never store what you can compute. Derived signals recompute on read and work on every adapter:

<Code lang="rust" code={`let count = cx.create_signal(2u32);

// Free function form:
let label = quoin_core::derived(&count, |n| format!("count = {n}"));
assert_eq!(label.get(), "count = 2");

// Method form (from SignalExt):
let doubled = count.map(|n| n * 2);

// Combine two signals into a tuple:
let both = quoin_core::zip(&a, &b);`} />

Keep derive closures cheap — they run on every read. When the computation is expensive, wrap it in a [`Memo`](/reference/derived/), which caches its output until the source value changes.

## React to changes with effects

The `effect!` macro runs a side effect whenever its dependencies change, with optional cleanup:

<Code lang="rust" code={`use quoin_macros::effect;

effect! {
    deps: [query],
    run: || {
        let data = fetch_data(&query.get());
        results.set(data);
    },
    cleanup: || {
        cancel_pending_request();
    }
}`} />

Each adapter lowers this to its native mechanism: `create_effect` + `on_cleanup` on Leptos, `use_effect` + `use_drop` on Dioxus, and run-on-execute with cleanup-on-drop on GPUI. See the [macros reference](/reference/macros/) for the legacy `watch: [...]` syntax and full semantics.

## Collapse bursts of writes with batching

When a handler writes several signals, wrap the writes in a batch so pull-based adapters (GPUI, Xilem) receive one re-render request instead of one per write:

<Code lang="rust" code={`cx.batch(|| {
    a.set(1);
    b.set(2);
});`} />

Fine-grained frameworks batch internally, so the call is safe on every adapter.

## Avoid leaking the framework

Two rules keep a hook portable:

1. **Do not name adapter types.** Use `C::Signal<T>` and trait methods; never `GpuiSignal`, `LeptosSignal`, or framework crates in hook signatures.
2. **Do not call framework APIs.** Rendering, windowing, and event listener registration belong in the view layer (or in the declarative macros, which expand per framework).

If you need `!Send` futures such as DOM-touching work, use the executor's `spawn_local` — see [Loading Async Data](/guides/async-data/).

## Next steps

- <LinkCard title="Loading Async Data" href="/guides/async-data/" description="Resources, spawned tasks, and timers in portable hooks." />
- <LinkCard title="Testing with quoin-testkit" href="/guides/testing/" description="Run your hooks headlessly with deterministic executors." />
- <LinkCard title="Signals Reference" href="/reference/signals/" description="Every method on Signal and SignalExt." />

---
title: Styling with Tailwind Classes
description: Style quoin_render! trees with Tailwind utility classes that compile to native styling on every backend.
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Badge, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

You will style declarative components with Tailwind utility classes. Class strings are parsed **at compile time** into Quoin's typed style IR and lowered to framework-native builder calls — there is no runtime class parsing and no string lookup in the emitted code.

**Prerequisites:** the `macros` feature (implied by any framework feature).

## Write classes in the tree

<Code lang="rust" code={`quoin_render! {
    div(class: "flex flex-col gap-4 p-4 bg-gray-900 text-white h-full") {
        div(class: "text-2xl font-bold hover:text-blue-400") { "Hello" }
        button(class: "px-4 py-2 bg-blue-600 rounded-md", on_click: move |_| increment()) {
            "Increment"
        }
    }
}`} />

On GPUI this compiles to method chains:

<Code lang="rust" code={`.flex().flex_col().gap(px(16.0)).p(px(16.0)).bg(rgb(0x111827))
.hover(|s| s.text_color(rgb(0x60a5fa)))`} />

The same class string lowers to each backend's native styling mechanism, so one source serves all frameworks.

## Know the supported vocabulary

The built-in parser (`quoin-style`) models this Tailwind subset:

- Flexbox direction, wrap, and alignment
- Gap, padding, margin
- Width/height (length values)
- Background and border colors (including theme tokens), border widths, corner radii
- Opacity, cursor, position offsets, overflow, shadows
- Text color, size, weight, alignment, and family
- The `hover:` state variant

**Unknown classes are a compile error.** The parser never silently drops a class it does not recognize; every backend must turn unrecognized classes into a `compile_error!` with a did-you-mean suggestion.

## Use theme tokens

Class names that map to [shadcn](https://ui.shadcn.com/) theme tokens (17 token names) resolve to baked colors — in the default engine, the shadcn dark-theme hex values. Tokens keep component styling consistent with the UCP `QuoinTheme` resolution.

## Extended engine for GPUI

<Badge text="Unreleased" variant="caution" />

The `gpui-rsx-classes` feature (enabled automatically by the `gpui` feature) routes classes Quoin does not know through the gpui-rsx class engine, which unlocks:

- The **full Tailwind 4 px-scale palette**, fractions, arbitrary values, and negative utilities
- Additional state variants: `focus:`, `focus-visible:`, `active:`, `group-hover:`, `group-active:`
- **Dynamic `class:` expressions** resolved at render time (unknown dynamic classes panic in strict mode)
- Custom vocabulary via an `rsx.toml` file next to your crate's `Cargo.toml`, with rebuild tracking

Classes Quoin already knows keep their byte-identical lowering under this flag, verified by parity tests.

## Escape hatch for GPUI-only subtrees

When you need raw gpui-rsx machinery inside a `quoin_render!` tree — for example to drop in a gpui-kit component — the `rsx` feature (implied by `gpui`) re-exports `rsx!`, `rsx_strict!`, `rsx_permissive!`, `rsx_tw!`, `rsx_fragment!`, `rsx_expand!`, `rsx_runtime!`, and `#[component]` from the `quoin` facade.

<Aside type="caution">
  The Floem adapter in this repository replaces the `muda` menu library with an API-compatible stub, so native menus are unsupported on Linux in this configuration.
</Aside>

## Next steps

- <LinkCard title="Declarative UI Macros" href="/guides/ui-macros/" description="Where class strings fit in component! and quoin_render!." />
- <LinkCard title="Feature Flags Reference" href="/reference/feature-flags/" description="The gpui-rsx-classes and rsx flags in detail." />

---
title: Testing with quoin-testkit
description: Run framework-agnostic hooks and stores headlessly with deterministic executors and update-count assertions.
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

You will test reactive business logic without a window manager or browser. `quoin-testkit` provides concrete, dependency-light implementations of the core traits designed for tests, so a hook written once runs in a plain `cargo test`.

**Prerequisites:** the `testkit` feature (or a direct dependency on `quoin-testkit`).

## Drive a hook with TestContext

<Code lang="rust" code={`use quoin_core::prelude::*;
use quoin_testkit::{ImmediateExecutor, TestContext};

fn use_counter<C: ReactiveContext>(cx: &C) -> C::Signal<u32> {
    cx.create_signal(0u32)
}

let mut cx = TestContext::with_executor(ImmediateExecutor);
let count = use_counter(&cx);
count.set(41);
count.update(|v| *v += 1);
assert_eq!(count.get(), 42);

// Update plumbing is observable:
assert_eq!(cx.updates().count(), 2, "set + update each requested a re-render");`} />

`TestContext` is a full `ReactiveContext` with update counting and a shared global store. `TestSignal` mutates bump the context's update counter, mirroring the pull-based adapters.

## Choose the right executor

| Executor | Behavior | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ImmediateExecutor` | Runs futures inline to completion; fully deterministic, blocking | Pure state machines, reducers, derived pipelines |
| `ThreadedExecutor` | One dedicated thread per future; real concurrency and abort semantics | Timers, channels, abort/detach tests |
| `TokioExecutor` *(feature `tokio`)* | Real tokio runtime | `#[tokio::test]` suites; supports paused time via `tokio::time::advance` |

<Aside type="caution">
  `ImmediateExecutor` cannot model mid-flight cancellation — futures finish before the handle exists. Use `ThreadedExecutor` (or the tokio one) when the logic under test awaits or exercises abort semantics.
</Aside>

## Assert re-render churn

`cx.updates()` records how many times the UI was asked to re-render. Pair it with `cx.batch(|| …)` to prove that batches collapse N writes into one update request:

<Code lang="rust" code={`cx.batch(|| {
    a.set(1);
    b.set(2);
});
assert_eq!(cx.updates().count(), 1);`} />

## Test framework-agnostic stores end to end

The repository ships two headless example suites you can read as templates:

- **todo-core** — a framework-agnostic todo store: `cargo test -p todo-core`
- **fetch-core** — resource-driven async search: `cargo test -p fetch-core`

Run the whole headless example suite (including the devtools demo) with `just test-headless-examples`.

## Next steps

- <LinkCard title="quoin-testkit Reference" href="/reference/testkit/" description="Every testkit type and executor in one table." />
- <LinkCard title="Tracing with quoin-devtools" href="/guides/devtools/" description="Record and inspect signal mutations, spawns, and update requests." />

---
title: Composing UCP Components
description: Build data tables, virtual lists, inputs, buttons, dropdowns, and tab bars through the framework-agnostic Universal Component Protocol.
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

You will build rich components — tables, virtual lists, dropdown menus, clipboard access — through the Universal Component Protocol (UCP), so the composition code stays framework-agnostic while an adapter crate supplies the native rendering.

**Prerequisites:** the `ui` feature (included by the `gpui` feature); for GPUI rendering the adapter ships `quoin-ui-gpui` automatically.

## Understand the two layers

UCP splits rich widgets into:

1. **Traits** in `quoin-ui` — abstract contracts such as `TableAdapter`, `VirtualListAdapter`, `ButtonAdapter`, `TextInputAdapter`, `DropdownMenuAdapter`, `TabBarAdapter`, and `Clipboard`.
2. **Adapter implementations** — concrete per-framework crates such as `quoin-ui-gpui` that know how to render the widget natively.

Your code talks to the traits; the framework feature pulls in the implementation.

## Render a button

`ButtonVariant` selects emphasis (`primary`, `ghost`, `destructive`) and density (`ComponentSize::Small | Medium | Large`):

<Code lang="rust" code={`use quoin_ui::{ButtonAdapter, ButtonVariant, ComponentSize};

let adapter = GpuiButtonAdapter::default();
let button = adapter.render(Some("Click Me".into()), ButtonVariant {
    primary: true,
    size: ComponentSize::Medium,
    ..Default::default()
});`} />

## Declare a sortable data table

Inside `quoin_render!`, the `data_table` element declares columns with keys, labels, and render closures; sorting and striping come from attributes:

<Code lang="rust" code={`data_table(rows: people, striped: true) {
    column(key: "name", label: "Name", render: |p: &Person| p.name.clone())
    column(key: "age",  label: "Age",  render: |p: &Person| p.age.to_string())
}`} />

`SortDirection` (`None | Asc | Desc`) models the per-column sort state on the `TableAdapter` side.

## Render large lists efficiently

`virtual_list` backs scrollable lists with the `VirtualListAdapter` contract so only visible rows render; scroll restoration is part of the node vocabulary (`scroll_restoration`).

## Read and write the clipboard

The `Clipboard` trait abstracts the system clipboard; the `clipboard_button` element wires a button that copies text and reports success:

<Code lang="rust" code={`clipboard_button(copy_text: "Copied!") { "Copy" }`} />

## Theme tokens

`QuoinTheme` resolves theme color tokens for adapters, so UCP components pick up consistent colors across light and dark appearances without hard-coded hex values in your code.

<Aside type="tip">
  Run the UCP demo to see every widget live: `just run-ucp-gpui` (or `just run-ucp-dioxus`) from the repository root.
</Aside>

## Next steps

- <LinkCard title="Universal Component Protocol Reference" href="/reference/ucp/" description="All traits, node types, and variant enums." />
- <LinkCard title="Declarative UI Macros" href="/guides/ui-macros/" description="Where UCP elements fit inside quoin_render! trees." />


---

---
title: Declarative UI Macros
description: Define components, render JSX-like trees, run effects, and bootstrap apps with component!, quoin_render!, effect!, and run_app!.
type: how-to
---

import { Aside, Badge, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

You will replace hand-written framework view code with Quoin's declarative macros. One syntax expands to native code for your chosen framework: a `Render` impl on GPUI, a `#[component]` function on Leptos and Dioxus.

**Prerequisites:** the `macros` feature (implied by any framework feature) — see [Installation](/guides/installation/).

## Define a component with `component!`

`component!` declares props, reactive state, globals, lifecycle hooks, actions, and the render tree in one block:

<Code lang="rust" code={`use quoin_macros::component;

component! {
    pub DemoApp {
        props {
            initial_count: u32 = 0,
        }
        state {
            count: u32 = initial_count,
            selected: String = "Option A".to_string(),
        }
        globals {
            theme: Theme,                  // automatically retrieved from context
            router: RouterState observe,   // observe = track changes
        }
        on_mount {
            log::info!("Component mounted");
        }
        on_unmount {
            log::info!("Component unmounted");
        }
        fn increment() {
            count.update(|c| *c += 1);
        }
        fn select_option(opt: String) {
            selected.set(opt);
        }
        render {
            let count_text = format!("Count: {}", count.get());
            quoin_render! {
                div(class: "flex flex-col gap-4 p-4 bg-gray-900 text-white") {
                    div(class: "text-2xl font-bold") { "Quoin Render Demo" }
                    div { count_text }
                    button(class: "px-4 py-2 bg-blue-600 rounded-md",
                        on_click: move |_| increment()) {
                        "Increment"
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}`} />

Framework output:

- **GPUI** — a `struct DemoApp` with a `Render` impl.
- **Leptos** — `#[component] fn DemoApp() -> impl IntoView`.
- **Dioxus** — `#[component] fn DemoApp() -> Element`.

State fields declared in `state` become signals; plain Rust code inside `render` runs each render pass.

## Write trees with `quoin_render!`

The render syntax is JSX-like with named attributes, conditional blocks, and loops:

<Code lang="rust" code={`use quoin_macros::quoin_render;

quoin_render! {
    div(class: "flex flex-col gap-4 p-4 bg-gray-900 text-white h-full") {
        div(class: "text-2xl font-bold hover:text-blue-400") { "Hello" }
        if[show_details] {
            div(class: "p-2 bg-gray-800 rounded-md") { details }
        }
        for[item in items] {
            div(class: "text-sm") { item.name.clone() }
        }
        tabs(active: active_tab, on_click: move |i| set_active(i)) {
            tab(index: 0, label: "Tab 1")
            tab(index: 1, label: "Tab 2")
        }
        data_table(rows: people, striped: true) {
            column(key: "name", label: "Name", render: |p: &Person| p.name.clone())
            column(key: "age",  label: "Age",  render: |p: &Person| p.age.to_string())
        }
        clipboard_button(copy_text: "Copied!") { "Copy" }
    }
}`} />

Beyond `div` and `button`, the element vocabulary includes the rich components the emitters support per framework: `tabs`, `data_table`, `virtual_list`, `dropdown_menu`, `input`, `checkbox`, `radio`, `switch`, `slider`, `icon`, `badge`, `tooltip`, `progress`, `skeleton`, `scroll_area`, `separator`, and `styled_text`. Handlers receive [typed events](/reference/events/), so the same handler source compiles on all backends.

## Run side effects with `effect!`

`effect!` has a structured form with dependencies, a run closure, and optional cleanup:

<Code lang="rust" code={`use quoin_macros::effect;

effect! { watch: [count], || println!("Count changed: {}", count.get()) }

effect! {
    deps: [query],
    run: || {
        let data = fetch_data(&query.get());
        results.set(data);
    },
    cleanup: || {
        cancel_pending_request();
    }
}`} />

- **Leptos** expands to `create_effect` + `on_cleanup`.
- **Dioxus** expands to `use_effect` + `use_drop`.
- **GPUI** executes the run closure and calls cleanup when the effect is dropped.

## Bootstrap with `run_app!`

One line mounts your component:

<Code lang="rust" code={`run_app!(MyComponent);                            // GPUI with default window options
run_app!(MyComponent, window_opts: custom_opts);  // GPUI with a custom window
run_app!(MyComponent);                            // Leptos/Dioxus mount to body`} />

## Define reusable elements with `quoin_element!`

<Badge text="Advanced" variant="caution" />

`quoin_element!` declares a named custom element with typed props, rendered through a `quoin_render!` closure:

<Code lang="rust" code={`quoin_element!("my-widget", { width: u32 }, |props| quoin_render! {
    div { "w" }
});`} />

<Aside type="note">
  The GPUI backend additionally re-exports the gpui-rsx escape hatch (`rsx!`, `rsx_strict!`, `#[component]`, …) under the `rsx` feature for GPUI-only subtrees inside `quoin_render!` render blocks — see the [styling guide](/guides/styling/#escape-hatch-for-gpui-only-subtrees).
</Aside>

import { Card, CardGrid, LinkButton, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Quoin is a framework-agnostic reactive abstraction layer for Rust. You write your business logic once against a small set of traits — signals, effects, async tasks, cancellation, global state — and the same code runs under GPUI, Leptos, Dioxus, Xilem, or Floem. ---

---
title: Batched Updates
description: API reference for batch::with, BatchGuard, and the notification suppression machinery shared by pull-based adapters.
type: reference
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

On pull-based adapters (GPUI, Xilem) every signal mutation calls `request_update()`. When a handler mutates several signals in a row this produces redundant re-render requests. Batching suppresses those intermediate notifications and issues a single update when the batch ends.

Import: `use quoin_core::prelude::*;` (the module) or `use quoin_core::batch;`

## API

| Item | Signature | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `batch::with` | `pub fn with<C, R>(cx: &C, f: impl FnOnce() -> R) -> R` where `C: ReactiveContext` | Runs `f` inside a batch scope and then requests a single UI update on `cx`. |
| `BatchGuard` | `pub struct BatchGuard` | RAII guard that increments the batch depth on creation and decrements it on drop. Create with `BatchGuard::enter()`. |
| `in_batch` | `pub fn in_batch() -> bool` | Returns `true` while inside a `with` scope. |
| `should_notify` | `pub fn should_notify() -> bool` | Used by adapter signal implementations: `true` when a mutation should notify (i.e. no batch is active). |

`ReactiveContextExt::batch` offers the same behavior as a method on the context: `cx.batch(\|\| …)`.

## How it works

A thread-local depth counter tracks nested batches. The signal implementations of the pull-based adapters consult `should_notify()` before invoking the update notifier. Fine-grained frameworks (Leptos, Dioxus, Floem) batch internally and ignore this mechanism, so the helper is safe to call everywhere.

## Example

<Code lang="rust" code={`let a = cx.create_signal(0u32);
let b = cx.create_signal(0u32);

quoin_core::batch::with(&cx, || {
    a.set(1);
    b.set(2);
});
assert_eq!((a.get(), b.get()), (1, 2));
// One re-render request instead of two.`} />

<Aside type="note">
  Batch bookkeeping is intentionally cheap (two thread-local accesses). Nesting works: only when the outermost batch ends is the update requested.
</Aside>

## Next steps

- <LinkCard title="Testing with quoin-testkit" href="/guides/testing/" description="Assert that a batch collapses N writes into one update." />
- <LinkCard title="The Reactivity Model" href="/explanation/reactivity-model/" description="Why pull-based adapters need batching and fine-grained ones do not." />

---
title: Cancellation Tokens
description: API reference for CancellationToken, CancelGuard, and the futures used for cooperative cancellation.
type: reference
---

import { Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

`CancellationToken` is a lightweight, cloneable token that signals cancellation to spawned futures. It integrates seamlessly with the async executors provided by UI frameworks and behaves identically on all five adapters.

Import: `use quoin_core::prelude::*;`

## CancellationToken methods

| Method | Signature | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `new` | `pub fn new() -> Self` | Creates a fresh token. |
| `cancel` | `pub fn cancel(&self)` | Marks the token cancelled and wakes all waiters. |
| `is_cancelled` | `pub fn is_cancelled(&self) -> bool` | Returns whether the token has fired. |
| `child_token` | `pub fn child_token(&self) -> Self` | Creates a token that cancels together with the parent but can also cancel independently. |
| `guard` | `pub fn guard(&self) -> CancelGuard` | RAII guard: cancels the token when dropped. |
| `cancelled` | `pub fn cancelled(&self) -> Cancelled<'_>` | Future that resolves when the token is cancelled. |
| `into_cancelled` | `pub fn into_cancelled(self) -> CancelledFuture` | Owned variant of `cancelled`. |
| `run_until_cancelled` | `pub fn run_until_cancelled<F: Future>(&self, future: F) -> RunUntilCancelled<'_, F>` | Races a future against the token. |

## Supporting types

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `CancelGuard` | RAII guard created by `guard()`; cancels the token when dropped. |
| `Cancelled<'a>` | Future resolving when the associated token is cancelled; created by `cancelled()`. |
| `CancelledFuture` | Owned variant created by `into_cancelled()`. |
| `RunUntilCancelled<'a, F>` | Resolves with `Some(output)` when the wrapped future finishes first, or `None` when the token wins. |

## Example

<Code lang="rust" code={`let token = CancellationToken::new();
executor.spawn({
    let token = token.clone();
    async move {
        while !token.is_cancelled() {
            do_work().await;
        }
        cleanup().await;
    }
});
token.cancel();

// Toolkit patterns:
let parent = CancellationToken::new();
let per_request = parent.child_token();        // cancels with the parent
let _guard = parent.guard();                   // RAII: cancels on drop
let value = parent.run_until_cancelled(work()).await;`} />

## Next steps

- <LinkCard title="Cancelling Work" href="/guides/cancelling-work/" description="Task-focused guide: token trees, guards, and races." />
- <LinkCard title="Executors & Tasks" href="/reference/executors/" description="spawn_with_token pairs an executor task with a token." />

---
title: Crates
description: API reference for the workspace layout — what every crate in the Quoin repository contains and which ones you depend on.
type: reference
---

import { Aside, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

Quoin is a Cargo workspace of small, focused crates. You normally depend on one of two crates only: `quoin` (applications) or `quoin-core` (framework-free libraries). The rest exist to keep that surface small.

## The crates you depend on

| Crate | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `quoin` | Facade — re-exports everything behind feature flags; the application entry point. |
| `quoin-core` | Core traits plus derived/resource/batch/local/pool machinery and the shared adapter infrastructure: `join` (join-handle lifecycle), `globals` (thread-local store), `NotifierSignal` (cell + batch-aware notifier). |

## Internal crates

| Crate | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `quoin-macros` | Proc-macro entry points: `component!`, `quoin_render!`, `quoin_element!`, `effect!`, `run_app!`. |
| `quoin-macros-core` | Macro parsing and code generation for every backend. |
| `quoin-style` | Typed style IR shared by every backend; compile-time Tailwind subset parsing. |
| `quoin-gpui` | GPUI adapter. |
| `quoin-leptos` | Leptos adapter. |
| `quoin-dioxus` | Dioxus adapter. |
| `quoin-xilem` | Xilem adapter. |
| `quoin-floem` | Floem adapter. |
| `quoin-ui` | Universal Component Protocol traits and node vocabulary. |
| `quoin-ui-gpui` | GPUI implementation of the UCP traits. |
| `quoin-testkit` | Headless testing: `TestContext` + deterministic executors. |
| `quoin-devtools` | Signal tracing and update logging. |
| `quoin-conformance` | Shared conformance test suite (30+ checks per adapter). |

## Supporting infrastructure

| Path | Role |
| --- | --- |
| `examples/` | Runnable demos per framework, plus headless e2e suites (`todo-core`, `fetch-core`, `devtools-demo`). |
| `interop-tests/` | Parity harness for the GPUI class engine (34/34 theme-token classes byte-identical, vocabulary-superset and Tailwind-scale gates). |
| `quoin-macros-tests/` | trybuild UI tests for macro diagnostics. |
| `quoin-grsx-compiletest/` | Compiles full engine expansions against the vendored GPUI stub. |
| `third_party/` | `gpui-stub` (fast type-checking of emitted chains) and `muda-stub` (Linux menu stand-in). |

## Workspace-wide policies

- Edition 2024, `rust-version = "1.88"`, version `0.1.0`.
- Lint policy defined once in the root manifest and inherited by every crate: `clippy::pedantic` + `clippy::all` + `missing_docs` with warnings denied by CI (`-D warnings`), `unsafe_code = "forbid"`, and `clippy::allow_attributes` denied — `#[allow(...)]` attributes are banned outright.
- Changelog generated from Conventional Commits by git-cliff.

<Aside type="note">
  The GPUI adapter depends on `gpui-pre` 0.3.10 (pinned). The `muda` replacement means native menus are unsupported on Linux in this configuration.
</Aside>

## Next steps

- <LinkCard title="Architecture" href="/explanation/architecture/" description="How the crates relate and where shared machinery lives." />
- <LinkCard title="Feature Flags" href="/reference/feature-flags/" description="Which flags pull in which crates." />

---
title: Derived Signals & Memos
description: API reference for derived(), map(), zip(), and Memo — computed views over signals on every adapter.
type: reference
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

A `Derived` signal wraps an existing `Signal` and computes its value lazily from the source signal on every read. It mirrors "computed" primitives from fine-grained reactive frameworks but works uniformly across all adapters: on Leptos, Dioxus, and Floem the source read inside the closure is tracked by the reactive graph; on GPUI and Xilem a source mutation triggers a re-render and the next read recomputes.

Import: `use quoin_core::prelude::*;`

## Functions

| Item | Signature | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `derived` | `pub fn derived<S, T, U, F>(source: &S, f: F) -> Derived<S, T, U, F>` where `F: Fn(&T) -> U + Clone + 'static` | Creates a read-only signal computing `U` from the source's `T`. The closure runs on every read — keep it cheap. |
| `zip` | `pub fn zip<A, B, TA, TB>(a: &A, b: &B) -> Zipped<A, B, TA, TB>` | Combines two signals into a read-only signal of their tuple, recomputed on each read. |
| `memo` | `pub fn memo<S, T, U, F>(source: &S, f: F) -> Memo<S, T, U, F>` | A derived signal that caches its last output until the source value changes. |

## Types

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `Derived<S, T, U, F>` | Read-only computed signal. Implements `Signal<U>`; reading clones the computed value. |
| `Zipped<A, B, TA, TB>` | Read-only signal combining two sources into a tuple. Created by `zip`. |
| `Memo<S, T, U, F>` | Caching derived signal: plain `derived` recomputes the closure on every read, `Memo` recomputes only when the source value differs from the last seen value. |

## SignalExt sugar

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `.map(f)` | Equivalent to `derived(self, f)` — chainable for multi-step computations. |

## Example

<Code lang="rust" code={`let count = cx.create_signal(2u32);

let label = count.map(|n| format!("count = {n}"));   // recomputed on read
assert_eq!(label.get(), "count = 2");

let doubled = quoin_core::derived(&count, |v| v * 2);
assert_eq!(doubled.get(), 4);

let both = quoin_core::zip(&a, &b);                  // tuple of two signals
assert_eq!(both.get(), (1, 2));

let expensive = quoin_core::memo(&source, heavy_transform);`} />

<Aside type="caution">
  Derived closures must be pure and cheap — they run on every read. Move expensive or allocation-heavy computations into a `Memo`, which caches until the source changes.
</Aside>

## Next steps

- <LinkCard title="Writing Portable Hooks" href="/guides/portable-hooks/" description="Where derived signals fit in portable hook design." />
- <LinkCard title="The Reactivity Model" href="/explanation/reactivity-model/" description="How pull-based and fine-grained adapters both support derived state." />

---
title: quoin-devtools
description: API reference for Instrumented, EventLog, EventKind, and the record helpers in quoin-devtools.
type: reference
---

import { Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

`quoin-devtools` is a framework-agnostic instrumentation layer. Wrap any adapter's `ReactiveContext` and every signal creation, read-triggering mutation, task spawn, and UI update request is recorded into an inspectable `EventLog`.

Import: `use quoin_devtools::{Instrumented, EventLog, EventKind, …};` or through the facade with the `devtools` feature.

## Module layout

| Module | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `event` | `Event`, `EventKind`, and the ring-buffer `EventLog` with its aggregate views. |
| `record` | The global log, the `QUOIN_TRACE` bootstrap, and the recording helpers shared by every wrapper. |
| `instrumented` | The `Instrumented` context, `TracedSignal`, and `TracedExecutor`. |

## Public API

| Item | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `Instrumented::wrap(raw_ctx, label)` | Drop-in wrapper around any adapter context; `label` names the session in events. |
| `global_log()` | Access to the process-wide `EventLog`. |
| `EventLog::dump()` | Prints a table to stderr. |
| `EventLog::hot_signals()` | Ranked mutation counts per signal. |
| `EventLog::events()` | Raw snapshot of `Event` values. |
| `EventLog::capacity()` | Ring capacity (default `DEFAULT_LOG_CAPACITY = 4096`). |
| `EventKind` | Event categories; `UpdateRequested` labels as `"update"`. |
| `enable()` / `disable()` / `enabled()` | Programmatic recording gate. |
| `init_from_env()` / `parse_trace_flag()` | The `QUOIN_TRACE=1` (or `on`) environment bootstrap. |
| `record()` / `snapshot()` / `thread_label()` | Shared recording helpers. |

## Zero-cost when disabled

Unless `enabled()` is turned on (default: the `QUOIN_TRACE` environment variable, or an explicit `enable()` call), the `Instrumented` wrapper short-circuits every recording call behind one relaxed atomic load, and no events are allocated.

The optional `tracing` feature forwards events into the `tracing` ecosystem.

## Example

<Code lang="rust" code={`use quoin_devtools::Instrumented;

let ctx = Instrumented::wrap(raw_ctx, "app");   // use ctx everywhere

// From a debug hotkey, a panel, or on exit:
quoin_devtools::global_log().dump();            // stderr table
quoin_devtools::global_log().hot_signals();     // ranked mutation counts
quoin_devtools::global_log().events();          // raw snapshot`} />

<Code lang="sh" code={`QUOIN_TRACE=1 ./myapp    # enable recording from the environment`} />

## Next steps

- <LinkCard title="Tracing with quoin-devtools" href="/guides/devtools/" description="Task-focused guide including the live xilem demo." />
- <LinkCard title="Testing with quoin-testkit" href="/guides/testing/" description="Deterministic headless testing that pairs well with tracing." />

---
title: Typed Events
description: API reference for the ev module — small value-type events that keep handler source identical on all five backends.
type: reference
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

The `ev` module (re-exported from the `quoin` facade as `quoin::ev`) defines typed events shared by every backend. Handlers receive small value types instead of framework-native event objects, so the same handler source compiles on all five adapters. Each adapter converts from its own event type through `From` impls that are `#[inline(always)]` in generated code.

Import: `use quoin::ev;` (facade) — the types are value structs.

## Payload contract

| Handler arity | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| Zero parameters (`\|\| …`) | Valid on every backend; the adapter calls the handler with no payload. |
| One parameter | Receives one of the payload structs below. During the transition period `()` still coerces for zero-arg handlers, which keeps existing GPUI source compiling unchanged. |

## Event types

| Type | Fired by | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Click` | Primary click / activation | Floem's `action` decorator and Xilem's button callbacks fire this. It is a unit-like struct (`Click {}`) with a `Click::new()` constructor. Adapters with richer pointer data widen the struct in later milestones without changing handler arity. |

## Example

<Code lang="rust" code={`// Zero-parameter handler — valid on every backend:
button(class: "px-4 py-2", on_click: || increment())

// One-parameter handler receiving the typed payload:
button(on_click: |ev: quoin::ev::Click| { /* ... */ })`} />

<Aside type="note">
  Because payloads are plain value types with `From` conversions in the generated code, a handler written against `ev` types never mentions a framework event type — that is what keeps the render tree portable.
</Aside>

## Next steps

- <LinkCard title="Declarative UI Macros" href="/guides/ui-macros/" description="Where event handlers attach to elements in quoin_render!." />
- <LinkCard title="Backend Parity" href="/explanation/backend-parity/" description="How identical handler semantics are verified across adapters." />


---

---
title: Executors & Tasks
description: API reference for the Executor trait, JoinHandle lifecycle, local (!Send) tasks, and portable timers.
type: reference
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

`Executor` spawns futures onto the framework's native async runtime. Every adapter implements the same trait and the same join-handle lifecycle, so task code is portable.

Import: `use quoin_core::prelude::*;`

## Executor methods

| Method | Signature | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `spawn` | `fn spawn<F>(&self, fut: F) -> JoinHandle<F::Output>` where `F: Future + Send + 'static`, `F::Output: Send + 'static` | Spawns a `Send` future on the framework runtime. |
| `sleep` | `fn sleep(&self, duration: Duration) -> SleepFuture` | Portable timer; futures-timer on native, browser timer on WASM. |

## ExecutorExt methods

| Method | Signature | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `spawn_with_token` | `fn spawn_with_token<F, Fut>(&self, f: impl FnOnce(CancellationToken) -> Fut) -> (JoinHandle<…>, CancellationToken)` | Creates a token, passes it to the future, and returns both the handle and the token — the fetch-and-cancel pattern in one call. |

## JoinHandle lifecycle

All adapters implement the same three lifecycle operations on `JoinHandle<T>`, plus `Future`:

| Operation | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `handle.await` | Waits for the result. The task runs to completion. |
| `handle.abort()` | Cancels the task at its next suspension point. Later awaits resolve with `Err(Canceled)`. |
| `handle.detach()` | Fire-and-forget: the task runs to completion, its result is discarded. |
| `drop(handle)` | Cancels the task (structured concurrency — no orphaned tasks mutating UI state). Use `detach()` when you explicitly want fire-and-forget. |

Cancellation is cooperative on the thread-based adapters (Leptos, Dioxus, Floem): the future stops at its next `.await` point. GPUI and Xilem cancel natively (dropping a GPUI `Task` / aborting a tokio task).

## Local (!Send) tasks

The `LocalExecutor` machinery handles futures that are not `Send`:

| Item | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `spawn_local` | Spawns a `!Send` future. On `wasm32` it runs on the browser main thread via `wasm_bindgen_futures`; on native it enters a deterministic thread-local FIFO queue. |
| `run_local_tasks` | Native driver: runs queued tasks to their next completion, one at a time. |
| `LocalTask` / `LocalJoinHandle` | Handles mirroring the join lifecycle: `abort` stops at the next suspension point, `detach` opts out of drop-cancellation, dropping cancels. |

GPUI does **not** implement `LocalExecutor` — its executor is `!Send` by design; use `Executor::spawn` there.

<Aside type="note">
  On `wasm32` targets, the Leptos and Dioxus executors run futures on the main thread via `wasm_bindgen_futures` instead of spawning threads.
</Aside>

## Standalone timer functions

| Item | Signature | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sleep` | `pub fn sleep(duration: Duration) -> SyncSleepFuture` | Free-function timer future, independent of any executor. |
| `SleepFuture` | — | The future returned by `Executor::sleep`. |
| `SyncSleepFuture` | — | The future returned by the free `sleep` function. |

## Example

<Code lang="rust" code={`let handle = executor.spawn(async {
    let data = fetch_from_api().await;
    signal.set(data);
});
let result = handle.await?;        // Err(Canceled) if aborted

let (h, token) = executor.spawn_with_token(|t| async move {
    while !t.is_cancelled() { do_work().await; }
});
executor.sleep(Duration::from_millis(250)).await;`} />

## Next steps

- <LinkCard title="Loading Async Data" href="/guides/async-data/" description="Task-focused guide covering resources, spawns, and timers." />
- <LinkCard title="Cancellation Tokens" href="/reference/cancellation/" description="The token types used by spawn_with_token and resources." />

---
title: Feature Flags
description: API reference for every cargo feature on the quoin facade, including dependencies between flags.
type: reference
---

import { Aside, Code, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

The `quoin` facade crate composes the ecosystem behind feature flags. **Exactly one framework feature may be enabled per crate** — Quoin enforces this with `compile_error!` diagnostics naming the mutually exclusive features.

## Framework features

| Feature | Pulls in | Also enables |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `gpui` | `gpui-pre`, `quoin-gpui`, `quoin-ui-gpui`, `quoin-macros` | `rsx`, `gpui-rsx-classes` |
| `leptos` | `quoin-leptos`, `quoin-macros` | — |
| `dioxus` | `quoin-dioxus`, `quoin-macros` | — |
| `xilem` | `quoin-xilem`, `quoin-macros` | — |
| `floem` | `quoin-floem`, `quoin-macros` | — |

## Tooling and protocol features

| Feature | Pulls in | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `macros` | `quoin-macros` | Macro entry points without a framework. |
| `ui` | `quoin-ui` | Universal Component Protocol traits. |
| `rsx` | `gpui-rsx` | Re-exports `rsx!`, `rsx_strict!`, `rsx_permissive!`, `rsx_tw!`, `rsx_fragment!`, `rsx_expand!`, `rsx_runtime!`, `#[component]` — the escape hatch for GPUI-only subtrees. Enabled automatically by `gpui`; standalone for raw-macro users. |
| `gpui-rsx-classes` | `quoin-macros` (forwarded as `quoin-macros/gpui-rsx-classes`) | Extended Tailwind engine for GPUI: full Tailwind 4 palette, extra state variants, dynamic `class:` expressions, `rsx.toml` custom tokens. Requires `macros` or any framework feature. |
| `testkit` | `quoin-testkit` | Headless testing re-exports. |
| `devtools` | `quoin-devtools` | Signal-tracing re-exports. |

## shadcn backing features

Use together with the matching framework feature; they activate the shadcn feature on the adapter crate **and** switch the macro emitter to target shadcn components:

| Feature | Requires |
| --- | --- |
| `leptos-shadcn` | `leptos` |
| `dioxus-shadcn` | `dioxus` |
| `floem-shadcn` | `floem` (expects a sibling `floem-shadcn` checkout consumed as a path dependency by `quoin-floem`) |

<Aside type="caution">
  The Floem shadcn backing is a standalone sibling checkout (v0.2.0 of the modified floem-shadcn tree), not a crates.io dependency. Cloning only the quoin repository is not enough to compile `floem-shadcn` builds — see the layout contract in the `quoin-floem` manifest.
</Aside>

## Example

<Code lang="toml" code={`[dependencies]
# Application targeting GPUI with UCP widgets, testkit, and devtools:
quoin = { version = "0.1", features = ["gpui", "testkit", "devtools"] }

# Framework-free hook library:
quoin-core = "0.1"`} />
